{{Short description|British mathematician (1908–1994)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2025}}
{{Use British English|date=January 2018}}
'''Ivor Malcolm Haddon Etherington''' [[FRSE]] (8 February 1908 – 1 January 1994)<ref name=rs-obit>{{Cite web |url=http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/fellowship/obits/obits_alpha/etherington_ivor.pdf |title=Biography of I. M. H. Etherington |access-date=31 March 2011 |archive-date=25 September 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060925162426/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/fellowship/obits/obits_alpha/etherington_ivor.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> was a British mathematician. He worked initially on [[general relativity]], and later on [[genetics]] where he introduced [[genetic algebra]]s.

==Life==

He was born in [[Lewisham]] in London, the posthumous son of the Baptist missionary Bruce Etherington (1874–1907)<ref>{{cite web |last1=The National Archives |title=Etherington, Bruce, (1874-1907), Baptist missionary |url=https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/c/F37377 |website=discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk}}</ref> and his missionary wife Annie Margaret. His father had died in Ceylon, leaving his mother and two older siblings to return to Britain alone. His mother remarried in 1913 to Edwin Duncombe de Rusett, a Baptist minister, but Ivor retained his original surname.

In 1921 the growing family moved out of London to [[Thorpe Bay]] on the [[Essex]] coast, where Ivor's step-father then founded the Thorpe Hall School for Boys. In 1922 Ivor was sent back to London to be educated at [[Mill Hill School]].<ref name=rs-obit/> Ivor was later educated at the [[University of Oxford]] and continued as a postgraduate at the [[University of Edinburgh]] where he received his doctorate.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Etherington|first=I. M. H.|date=1932|title=On relativistic cosmology and on the definition of distance in general relativity|website=Edinburgh Research Archive|url=https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/32130|language=en}}</ref> He later became a professor of mathematics at the same university.

Etherington was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1934. His proposers were [[E. T. Whittaker|Sir Edmund Whittaker]], [[Herbert Westren Turnbull]], [[Edward Thomas Copson]] and David Gibb. He won the Society's Keith Medal for 1955–57.<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=[[Royal Society of Edinburgh|The Royal Society of Edinburgh]]|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|access-date=18 April 2016|archive-date=24 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130124115814/http://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp1.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> His doctoral students include [[Henryk Minc]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=299944|name=Ivor Malcolm Haddon Etherington}}</ref>

On his retirement in 1974, Etherington moved with his wife to [[Easdale]] on the Scottish west coast, where the family had always had a holiday home. He died on 1 January 1994.<ref name=rs-obit/>

==Family==

He married Elizabeth (Betty) Goulding in 1934. They had two daughters, Donia and Judy. When Betty died in 1982, Donia came to care for her father.<ref name=rs-obit/>

During [[World War II]] he and his wife aided 32 German refugees, giving many shelter in their own home.<ref name=rs-obit/>
